1	# Portable settings and one-time ADB recovery pilot
2	
3	Intent: recover all configuration from the owner's prior debuggable Farhan installation without changing or uninstalling it, then provide normal file-based settings export/import that survives app signing-key changes. Notification and usage history are explicitly excluded. Base: c36faf1. Pilot branch: pilot/settings-portability; prior notification pilot remains on rework.
4	
5	## Scope and storage
6	
7	Source is user-authorized ADB access to a debuggable package. Wireless pairing grants shell, not root; `run-as` must succeed before export. A separate rescue APK must coexist with old and new Farhan. Package and user are explicit, default personal user 0; never assume a work-profile installation. Default package ly.com.tahaben.farhan_alpha, editable validated Android package name. No arbitrary command UI, uninstall, clear-data, package replacement, or source-file writes.
8	
9	Settings span shared_prefs/shared_pref.xml, files/datastore/farhan_data_store.preferences_pb, and configuration rows in Room (apps_db and TimeLimitEntity; confirm any older DB names). Preferences cover notification app/channel/category overrides, priority locks, schedule/budgets/delivery cadence, queue preferences, exceptions, launcher/time limits/delayed launch, grayscale, scroll blocker, theme, main switches and other user configuration. Launcher activity rows include package/activity/user-serial; only restore to the same device/user initially, warn on unmatched activities. Notification/usage/launch-attempt/day-update tables are not settings. No live notification PendingIntents, runtime proxies, permission grants or Keystore keys are transferable.
10	
11	The rescue app pairs to same-device wireless debugging (Android 11+) using pairing port/code and then connection port. Pair code is entered locally, never logged. Reuse a pinned existing ADB client, not a new protocol implementation. Pair credentials stay private to rescue and backup is disabled for rescue. No Shizuku dependency. Button explicitly stops the source app to obtain consistent files; it then reads with run-as over non-PTY binary streams. Preserve source DB+WAL while temporarily decoding SQLite in rescue-private cache, select configuration rows only, delete all raw artifacts on success/cancel/error/next startup. Never export notification content. Only source-data copies are opened by SQLite; the original is never opened for writing. Validate package/user/path arguments; never derive shell syntax from file contents.
12	
13	## Portable file contract
14	
15	One versioned UTF-8 JSON format shared by normal export and rescue conversion; source package/version/user/device metadata plus typed preference maps (boolean/int/long/float/double/string/string-set as applicable to storage) and explicit configuration row lists. Integers retain precision; no float conversion of longs. String-set ordering is deterministic. DataStore is decoded to typed values, not an opaque protobuf in the public file. Legacy SharedPreferences XML is decoded strictly, retaining known configuration with original types; unknown keys are surfaced/preserved as inert recovery data rather than silently lost or executed. Include schedule information in a readable versioned representation or existing validated JSON, with legacy migration through existing schedule logic; no silent default on a bad schedule. Current budget aggregates may be retained; spend detail/history excluded. Natural day/window reset must continue to apply.
16	
17	Bound input sizes/counts before allocation, reject unknown format version, malformed/duplicate keys, invalid types/ranges, corrupt/truncated data, unexpected archive paths, and unsupported required settings before any destination mutation. Export/import preview names source and counts and reports omitted secrets/device grants. Reject source=destination in rescue. Full settings replace is explicit; preserve notification/history tables and unrelated current app internal state. Do not blindly copy all SharedPreferences into a fresh app.
18	
19	Automation credential/receipt and recovery/ADB secrets never appear in portable files. Restored automation is disabled and needs a new credential. No notification/usage text or app credentials in logs, errors or test fixtures. Backups are ordinary user-chosen documents and contain private configuration; no network upload. Use Storage Access Framework CreateDocument/OpenDocument, no broad storage permission.
20	
21	## Import lifecycle and atomicity
22	
23	Settings are distributed across SharedPreferences, DataStore, Room and in-memory caches. A sequence of setters while the listener runs is not an acceptable atomic import. Stage and fully validate a restore first. Require a visible apply-and-close/reopen flow; perform the actual restore before normal app initialization on next launch, while stores/workers/listener are quiescent. The preparation step must open/create the current Room schema before staging so startup restoration never creates a partial DB schema.
24	
25	Use a durable import journal with previous and desired complete configuration. Every phase is idempotent across process death. On startup, apply all components before Hilt-created stores, WorkManager or user screens can read them. A store failure selects rollback durably, restores all previous components, and reports failure. If rollback itself fails, retain journal and block normal operation with recovery UI/retry; never present success or run with half-restored configuration. SQL writes touch only the explicit configuration tables in one transaction. Do not replace the Room database or historical tables. Offline DataStore replacement occurs only before its singleton exists; portable typed values must be prepared correctly with the public DataStore API. Receipt/journal live under no_backup and are excluded from export. Prefer a simpler design if it provides the same construction and tests.
26	
27	## Pilot tests and evidence
28	
29	Red tests must exercise production codec/converter and import coordinator ports: literal legacy XML + typed DataStore values/config rows -> exact portable values; lossless long/string-set behavior; explicit app/category/channel/schedule/budget settings preserved; histories/secrets excluded with positive controls; malformed/version/limit/type failures leave all stores unchanged; valid replace preserves history; failure on each store triggers rollback; crash/replay before/after phase boundaries converges without partial visible state; failures preserve recoverability and never acknowledge success. Test actual production seam, not a second algorithm. WHY/CLAIM/catches on each distinct case. Focused, bounded tests only; JVM tests where possible.
30	
31	Runtime checks: old debuggable synthetic app data -> helper -> portable JSON -> new signed app -> matching configuration, with original source intact. Private owner data is not required in test logs or repo. Actual owner recovery requires owner pairing input/device interaction; no assumption that it already ran. The rescue APK should first be used to secure a backup before any signing-key uninstall/reinstall.
32	
33	Defaults: settings only per owner; full explicit replace; personal user 0; secrets excluded; readable JSON; import requires cold start for consistency. This is a pilot, durability bar 9, correctness/security/architecture/legibility 6 pending stronger owner preferences. Physical wireless pairing and UI proof are separate from compile/JVM proof. No push/PR authorized. Boat is below reserve; the previous ten-minute exception is exhausted. Prepare code/tests first and investigate local/queued build route before requesting another exception.

2	name: technical-excellence
3	description: >-
4	  Design and code standards for work that must stay correct: rich interfaces
5	  (errors, reason, invariants, parity tests), cited claims with grep-able ids,
6	  deep modules, a project lexicon with disciplined naming, type-level safety
7	  (invalid states unrepresentable, monoids, exhaustive matching), and a
8	  threat-model check on security. Use when designing an abstraction, writing or
9	  reviewing code or comments, naming things, or judging a review finding.
10	  Companions: test-quality (proving it), build-loop (the workflow).
11	---
12	
13	# technical-excellence
14	
15	Standards for what the code says and how it is shaped.
16	
17	| Skill | Load it when |
18	|---|---|
19	| `test-quality` | Writing or reviewing the tests that prove an interface, claim or invariant here. |
20	| `build-loop` | The work is multi-phase, or a cross-model review will judge it. Its review step uses sections 6 and 7 below. |
21	
22	First rule: **when in Rome.** Follow the repo's conventions (AGENTS.md,
23	existing style, lexicon) before anything below. Apply this skill where the repo
24	is silent.
25	
26	## 1. Rich interfaces
27	
28	An interface is more than signatures. Each abstraction documents:
29	
30	| Part | Says |
31	|---|---|
32	| Error detail | What can fail, and how it is reported (type, code, null, exception). Callers must be able to handle each case without reading the body. |
33	| Reason | Why it exists. What breaks or duplicates if it is removed. |
34	| Invariants | What is always true before, during and after calls. |
35	| Mating parts | If it has a second or third counterpart (writer/reader, encoder/decoder, client/server), name them. |
36	
37	**Mated parts need parity tests** proving both sides agree: round trip, plus
38	independent fixtures (see `test-quality`, parity and oracles). A pair that is
39	only tested against each other's constants proves nothing.
40	
41	## 2. Claims are cited
42	
43	Module-level comments and comments above code blocks contain verifiable
44	claims ("this is O(n)", "the device sends big-endian", "idempotent",
45	"commit happens before ACK"). Every such claim is anchored and sourced.
46	
47	Convention (adapt the comment syntax to the language):
48	
49	```
50	// CLAIM(ack-order): the commit completes before the ACK is sent [spec §4.2; ack_order_test]
51	...
52	// ↳ CLAIM(ack-order)
53	ack(token);
54	```
55	
56	- The comment states a **verifiable** claim and its **source or proof** in
57	  brackets: a spec section, capture file, proof sketch, or test name.
58	- The code the claim governs carries `↳ CLAIM(<id>)`.
59	- A maintainer changing that code greps the id, finds the claim and its
60	  proof, and re-checks it.
61	- Tests that prove the claim name the id in their why (`test-quality`).
62	- Ids are short, unique, stable. Unprovable "claims" are opinions: label them
63	  as such or delete them. A comment with no source is a rumor.
64	
65	## 3. Deep modules
66	
67	Prefer a simple interface over a substantial implementation. Few entry
68	points, few parameters, no leaked internals. Smells: shallow wrappers that
69	forward one call; interfaces as long as the body; callers that must know
70	call order. Hide the complexity; do not spread it across callers.
71	
72	## 4. Lexicon and naming
73	
74	Keep a project lexicon (a glossary doc: term, meaning, where it lives). Name
75	code in correspondence with it. Add a term to the glossary when you coin one;
76	do not use two words for one concept.
77	
78	Outside any convention:
79	
80	- Clear names, **no abbreviations**.
81	- 1-2 primary words, plus optional small words (determiners, prepositions):
82	  `rowsToPrune`, `nightOfRecord`.
83	- Be deliberate about grammar:
84	  - functions and methods: verbs (`parseFrame`); predicates read as
85	    questions (`isFinalized`, `hasPendingWrite`);
86	  - values and types: nouns (`dayLabel`, `HistoryToken`);
87	  - qualifiers: adjectives (`pendingRows`);
88	  - tense shows state: `committedRows` (done), `rowsToCommit` (not yet).
89	- Name by how the value is used, not its type. Avoid vague names such as
90	  `value`, `data`, `result`, `tmp`. A function that sums two numbers returns
91	  `sum`; a truly generic result is `returnValue`.
92	
93	## 5. Type-level safety first
94	
95	Algorithmic and algebraic design shrinks runtime checks, tests and review.
96	Reach for these before adding a check:
97	
98	| Tool | Effect |
99	|---|---|
100	| Make invalid states unrepresentable (sum types, non-empty lists, state enums carrying only valid fields) | The bug cannot compile. No test or review needed. |
101	| Newtypes / branded types (`LocalDayLabel` vs `UtcTimestamp`, `Milliseconds` vs `Seconds`) | Mixed-up units and ids fail to compile. |
102	| Exhaustive matching, no default branch | Adding a case forces every consumer to be updated. |
103	| Monoids (identity, associative combine) for accumulators | Split-merge equals single pass; parallelism and incrementality are safe. Prove laws with property tests (`test-quality`). |
104	| Parse, don't validate: convert raw input to a checked type once, at the boundary | Inner code never re-checks. |
105	| Smart constructors, private fields | Invariants hold by construction. |
106	
107	If a runtime check or a test exists only to catch an invalid state a type
108	could forbid, change the type.
109	
110	## 6. Security stance review
111	
112	Security judgments are made against a **threat model**, never by reflex.
113	
114	1. Use the project's existing framework (a residual-risk framework, AGENTS.md
115	   invariants, an existing model).
116	2. If none exists, write a short `THREAT_MODEL.md`: assets, actors, trust
117	   boundaries, in scope, out of scope. Leave it UNCOMMITTED unless the user
118	   says otherwise.
119	3. Question the stance itself: which assets matter most, who can reach which
120	   boundary, what is knowingly accepted. Record accepted risks with a reason.
121	4. For each security-relevant change or review comment, decide: real exposure
122	   under the model, hardening nicety, or out of scope. State which and why.
123	5. Where a project limits reviewers to correctness findings, honor that for
124	   what you ask of them, but still assess security yourself.
125	
126	## 7. Judging review findings
127	
128	A finding is not a nit because it is small. Check it against: the claim it
129	contradicts (section 2), the invariant it breaks (section 1), the type that
130	could prevent it (section 5), and the threat model (section 6). Then apply
131	the smallest fix, with a test that fails without it (`test-quality`).
132

1	---
2	name: test-quality
3	description: >-
4	  What makes a test worth keeping, and the catalog of ways tests pass while
5	  proving nothing. Every test states its WHY (and CLAIM id); co-located tests;
6	  monoid laws, model-based state-machine properties, oracles, reviewed goldens,
7	  parity tests for mated interfaces; cheap manual mutation checks and periodic
8	  mutation tooling; explicit tautology hunting; plus the full failure-mode
9	  catalog with detection hints and fixes (tautology, over-mocking, asserting
10	  current behavior, happy-path only, host-timezone dependence, skipped
11	  fixtures, source-grep guards, wrong-layer pins, shared-table round trips).
12	  Use when writing tests, reviewing a test diff, fixing a red test, auditing a
13	  suite, or when a subagent (rg-implement or build-loop red phase) hands back
14	  tests. Companions: technical-excellence, build-loop.
15	---
16	
17	# Test quality
18	
19	A green run says nothing about whether a test can fail. For every test you
20	write or review, answer one question: **if the bug came back, would this go
21	red?** If you can't name the bug it catches, it's hollow.
22	
23	| Skill | Load it when |
24	|---|---|
25	| `technical-excellence` | The test proves an interface, invariant or CLAIM, or a type could make the test unnecessary. Source of the CLAIM convention and mated-part (parity) rule. |
26	| `build-loop` | You are in a red/green run or a review round. Its red gate uses this skill; review findings about tests are judged with it. |
27	
28	## 1. Every test says why
29	
30	The reason a test exists is hard to recall later. Annotate each test with a
31	short WHY: the bug, rule, incident or claim it guards.
32	
33	```
34	// why: a partial chunk must never be ACKed (invariant 3.1; regression of the
35	//      2026-09 early-ack bug). Fails if commit moves after ack.
36	// proves: CLAIM(ack-order)
37	```
38	
39	- A test proving a CLAIM (see `technical-excellence`) names its id, so the
40	  claim's grep finds its proof.
41	- No why, no keep: a test whose purpose nobody can state is a deletion
42	  candidate.
43	- Expected values show their derivation (spec section, capture, arithmetic).
44	
45	## 2. Placement
46	
47	Co-locate tests with the code they test, unless the repo's convention says
48	otherwise (when in Rome). A test beside its module shows what the abstraction
49	is, travels with it, and is deleted with it. Cross-cutting and end-to-end
50	suites live apart, and say so in their why.
51	
52	## 3. Techniques worth using
53	
54	### Monoids and accumulators
55	If a type combines (`combine`, identity element), property-test the laws:
56	
57	| Law | Property |
58	|---|---|
59	| Identity | `combine(x, empty) == x == combine(empty, x)` |
60	| Associativity | `combine(combine(a,b),c) == combine(a,combine(b,c))` |
61	| Commutativity | `combine(a,b) == combine(b,a)` (only if claimed) |
62	| Split-merge | for any split of the input, `combine(fold(left), fold(right)) == fold(whole)` (single pass equals chunked/parallel/incremental) |
63	
64	Generate inputs randomly with a fixed seed; shrink failures.
65	
66	### State machines
67	Model-based property tests: a small pure model of the intended states and
68	transitions; generate random command sequences; apply to model and real
69	system; assert observable state agrees after every step, and that illegal
70	transitions are refused. Include crash/rollback and retry commands.
71	
72	### Oracles
73	Expected values come from something independent of the code under test:
74	- a slow, obviously-correct reference implementation;
75	- a hand-computed fixture (arithmetic in a comment);
76	- a real capture or spec table, decoded field by field.
77	Beware a shared oracle: incremental-vs-forced parity can pass while both
78	paths inherit the same regression. Keep an independently derived fixture next
79	to the parity test.
80	
81	### Goldens
82	High quality means: reviewed by a person, minimal (smallest input that shows
83	the behavior), deterministic (zone, clock, seed, locale pinned), explained
84	(why: what it pins, version or pin it was generated at). Regeneration is a
85	deliberate, flagged act, never silent. A golden nobody inspected is mode 12.
86	Retain exact comparison for a fixed version; do not hide change behind a
87	blanket tolerance.
88	
89	### Parity tests for mated interfaces
90	Writer/reader, encoder/decoder, client/server: test both against literal
91	bytes or messages from the spec or a real capture, field by field, not just
92	against each other. Round-trip tests are a supplement, never the proof.
93	Dedupe parity corpora and report the real unique count.
94	
95	## 4. Mutation checks
96	
97	**Cheap manual mutations (do these every time).** Pick 3-5 spots in the code
98	under test, mutate one at a time, run the focused tests:
99	
100	| Mutation | If still green |
101	|---|---|
102	| Flip a condition (`<` to `<=`, `&&` to `\|\|`, negate) | Boundary or branch untested |
103	| Delete a line or a call | That line is unproven; or the test is at the wrong layer |
104	| Change a constant (offset, threshold, default) | Value not asserted exactly |
105	| Swap two arguments or an ordering | Order not pinned |
106	
107	Use the result to decide: more tests needed, or tests that prove nothing
108	(remove them). Revert every mutation; never commit one.
109	
110	**`# catches:` and post-green spot mutations (build-loop red/green).** Each
111	red test carries a `# catches: <a plausible wrong implementation this fails>`
112	line. If you cannot name one, the test is likely a tautology; rewrite or drop
113	it. After green, the orchestrator applies 2-3 of those named wrong
114	implementations and checks the matching tests go red. A green implementer that
115	edits a red test says so in its report; the edit becomes a review finding.
116	
117	**Mutation tool, periodically.** If the stack has one (for example Stryker,
118	mutmut, cargo-mutants, PIT), run it every so often on a stable module.
119	Surviving mutants show gaps. Tests that kill no unique mutant and duplicate
120	another test's kills are candidates to prune, which keeps the standard suite
121	small and fast.
122	
123	## 5. Hunt tautology explicitly
124	
125	Before approving any test, ask of each assertion: *can this expression be
126	false given any implementation?* Tautology signs: value compared to itself;
127	mock returns what it was told; expected computed by the function under test;
128	a literal's length asserted on the literal; a test of a pasted copy; a
129	mirrored formula. Mode 1 and 5 below, with fixes. For tautology, the
130	tool is the "revert the fix" mutation.
131	
132	## 6. The mutation check that catches most failure modes
133	
134	Mentally (or actually) mutate the code under test and see if the test fails:
135	
136	1. Revert the fix the test claims to pin. Still green? The test is wrong.
137	2. Delete the call site the test claims to cover (not the helper: the place
138	   production calls it). Still green? Wrong layer.
139	3. Empty the list, set or config the test iterates over. Still green? Vacuous.
140	4. Run it under `TZ=UTC` and under a DST zone. Different result, or a skip?
141	   Host-dependent.
142	5. Remove the fixture file. Skip with no CI failure? It never runs in CI.
143	
144	Before calling a suite done, do 1 for at least the tests whose names claim a
145	bug.
146	
147	## 7. Classic modes
148	
149	| # | Mode | Looks like | Fix |
150	|---|---|---|---|
151	| 1 | Tautology | Value compared to itself; mock returns what it was told; expected computed by the function under test; `hasLength(12)` on a 12-item literal; `isNotNull` on a tear-off | Expected value from the spec or a hand calculation |
152	| 2 | Over-mocking | The engine/unit under test is stubbed; only fakes run | Mock the clock, network, platform. Never the unit |
153	| 3 | Asserts current behavior | Magic numbers with no derivation (`9.03`, `closeTo(50, 8)`); comment-free goldens | Show the arithmetic in a comment, or cite the spec/capture the value came from |
154	| 4 | Happy path only | No empty, null, zero, negative, NaN, boundary, duplicate, truncated, error, or thin-input case | List the edge cases before writing the first test |
155	| 5 | Mirrored implementation | Test re-implements the formula, or tests a pasted copy of a private helper | Hand-computed constants; test the real symbol |
156	| 6 | Coverage theater | Code runs, nothing meaningful is asserted; benchmark tests with no `expect` | Every test asserts a concrete value |
157	| 7 | Existence only | `isNotNull`, `isNotEmpty`, `returnsNormally`, `greaterThan(0)`, `isA<T>()`, `verify(called)` where the exact value is known | Assert the value. If the seeded row count is 3, assert 3 |
158	| 8 | Weakened during a fix | Exact value became a range; case deleted; `skip:` added; tolerance widened | Treat any loosened test in a fix diff as a red flag. Change the code, not the test. `git log -p` the test file |
159	| 9 | Volume over quality | Dozens of near-identical cases; parity corpora where the same records repeat (978 unique of 2,934) | Fewer, distinct cases; dedupe corpora and report the real count |
160	| 10 | Confidently wrong | Expected value contradicts the spec, docs, or the test's own earlier assertion | Flag uncertain inputs instead of guessing |
161	| 11 | Unreadable failure | `expect(cond, isTrue)` with no `reason:`; byte lists without hex | Match on the value, or add `reason:` naming expected vs actual |
162	| 12 | Blind golden | Snapshot regenerated by an env var; nobody inspected it | Golden only reviewed output; note who checked it and against what |
163	
164	## 8. Modes the classic list misses
165	
166	These came up across three repos, often in tests that looked careful.
167	
168	**Host-timezone dependence.** DST and local-vs-UTC tests that only bite when
169	the machine's zone differs from UTC, or that `markTestSkipped` unless
170	`TZ == America/Denver`. CI runners are UTC, so the check is vacuous there.
171	Calls that default to the host zone (no offset argument) also flip results
172	by zone. Fix: pin the zone inside the test, or pass the offset explicitly.
173	Never derive the expected value with the same `toLocal()` the code uses.
174	Run CI as a matrix: UTC plus one DST zone.
175	
176	**Silently skipped fixtures.** The test skips when a data file is absent,
177	and that file is gitignored or lives outside the repo. CI never runs it, yet
178	it's often the only end-to-end or real-capture test. Fix: commit a small
179	fixture, or make the skip loud in CI (fail when `CI` is set). Same for sibling
180	checkouts: a guard that skips unless `../analytics` exists, when the real
181	directory is `../openstrap-analytics`, has never run anywhere. Golden groups
182	that skip because the golden directory is absent are the same mode.
183	
184	**Source-grep guards.** "Ordering is untouched" checks that two identifiers
185	appear in a file; "prune order" checks `indexOf` positions; a "no 86400 s"
186	guard covers 22 hand-listed files and misses `86_400`. These pass if a comment
187	contains the string, if the code is reordered in a way the regex can't see,
188	or if the bug lands in an unlisted file. Fix: drive the behavior (seed a
189	partial day, prune, assert rows survive). Keep grep guards only as a backstop,
190	cover the whole tree, and include a positive control proving the pattern
191	matches something. A whole-tree scan for a new caller or forbidden dependency
192	is the legitimate kind (an audit of 88 guard files kept 18 of this type,
193	converted 48 to behavior tests, and removed 22).
194	
195	**Pins dead code or the wrong layer.** The test exercises a pure helper, but
196	production reads the value through a different path. Real examples: a
197	readiness-flash test pinning a getter with zero callers; a freeze test that
198	covers the pure function but not where the screen reads or the engine writes;
199	a race test that never imports the service and tests `List.remove`; an "edge
200	half" test that only calls the sibling library; "the stager only runs inside
201	`Isolate.run`" checked by two strings anywhere in the file (output parity is
202	not execution placement). Fix: test through the seam the user hits, or add a
203	test that the production path calls the helper.
204	
205	**Shared-table round trip.** The test builds a frame at offset 13 and the
206	parser reads offset 13 from the same constant. A wrong offset passes. Fix:
207	literal bytes from a real capture or the spec, decoded field by field. When a
208	real capture exists, assert every field you can hand-decode, not just the
209	version byte or the first 4 of 8 token bytes.
210	
211	**Capability tested once, wired N times.** The new decoder is tested
212	directly, but two other entry points still call the old one. Fix: count the
213	entry points and test each, or add a guard that they all route through one.
214	
215	**Iterating over the current set.** `for (op in dangerousCmds) expect(...)`
216	stays green when the set is emptied or an item is dropped. Fix: pin the
217	required members by name, then loop.
218	
219	**Conditional assertions.** `if (row != null) expect(...)` passes with nothing
220	checked. Fix: assert the precondition first.
221	
222	**Assertions on absence with no positive control.** "Nothing was written"
223	checked via `total_changes` or a log line, without proving the probe moves on
224	a real write. A no-bounce check that matches log wording passes if the log is
225	reworded. Fix: show the probe detects the positive case in the same test.
226	
227	**Test-only configuration.** The test runs with thresholds (300/200/200) that
228	differ from shipped defaults (200/150/750). Fix: test the shipped defaults,
229	plus overrides as separate cases.
230	
231	**Change-detector literals.** `expect(kAlgoVersion, 104)` or a literal SHA.
232	It fails on every bump and catches nothing. Fix: assert the property you care
233	about (the pinned commit contains the cited change).
234	
235	**Real time.** `DateTime.now()`, real `Future.delayed` sleeps, and "nothing
236	yet" checked after 300 ms. Flaky near midnight and on slow runners; a real
237	one-minute wait inside a correctness test costs a minute on every run. Fix:
238	`fakeAsync` with `withClock`, or inject the clock.
239	
240	**Tolerance that spans the plausible universe.** VO2max accepted in 30-70
241	when the hand value is 49.14; RMSSD up to 500 ms; one-sided bounds with no
242	upper limit; `closeTo(50, 8)` where the formula gives exactly 50 at z=0, so
243	weights and signs go untested. Fix: tolerance sized to numeric error, not to
244	"looks reasonable."
245	
246	## 9. Domain checks worth adding wherever they apply
247	
248	- **Absent input.** Missing or thin input returns null, absent, or "—", never
249	  a default or a value derived from another metric.
250	- **Idempotence.** Run the computation three times with slightly more data;
251	  the persisted value stays stable. Append a duplicate day; the baseline
252	  doesn't move.
253	- **Failure paths.** Every flag set on the happy path is cleared on error,
254	  timeout, and give-up.
255	- **Durability ordering.** Commit before acknowledge, tested by driving the
256	  real engine and observing the order, including a rollback case.
257	- **Ambient state.** Globals that change output are re-armed inside isolate
258	  closures, and a test shows output changes when they're set.
259	
260	## 10. Grounding from suite audits
261	
262	Two audits of a large suite (about 14,000 test blocks across three repos)
263	produced these lessons; use them to prioritize.
264	
265	| Lesson | What to do |
266	|---|---|
267	| Many tests never ran: TZ-gated, fixture-gated, sibling-checkout-gated skips | Fix execution first (TZ matrix, committed fixtures, fail-on-skip under `CI`) before writing new tests. |
268	| Invariant gaps sat next to thousands of passing tests (ACK ordering, prune safety, RAM-only streams, dangerous-opcode lists) | Map each written invariant to a behavioral test that drives the real engine; grep-guards do not count. |
269	| Source-grep guards: 88 audited, about a fifth worth keeping | Keep whole-tree dependency/caller bans with a positive control; convert ordering/token greps to behavior; delete comment-proximity checks. |
270	| Shared-oracle limit: incremental-vs-forced parity passes when both inherit a regression | Keep an independent versioned fixture beside parity tests; store the generating algorithm version/pin with each golden. |
271	| Characterization suites overlap controller tests, but not fully | Trim case by case; do not delete wholesale. Check what the higher layer still uniquely covers (real claims, persistence, races). |
272	| Real waits dominated cost (a 60 s breathing session, fixed 5 s reply windows) | Inject clocks and parameterize windows; keep timing out of correctness tests. |
273	| Vacuous tolerances and `greaterThan(0)` everywhere | Sweep mechanically after reworks, not before, to avoid collisions. |
274	| A test endorsed behavior a written invariant forbids | When a test and an invariant conflict, stop and ask the owner. Do not "fix" either silently. |
275	| Golden baseline failed after an algorithm version bump; nothing recorded which version made it | Diff old vs new at field level; rebaseline only if all changes are the intended ones; store version and pin beside the golden. |
276	
277	## 11. When writing tests (especially as a subagent)
278	
279	- Write expectations from the spec before reading the implementation's
280	  output. Show the arithmetic.
281	- State each test's why and CLAIM id (section 1).
282	- List inputs you're unsure about instead of inventing expected values.
283	- Confirm each new test fails against the broken code (red first).
284	- Never loosen an existing assertion to make a fix pass. If it must change,
285	  say why in the commit message.
286	
287	## 12. When reviewing
288	
289	Read assertions before the green checkmark. For each test, name the bug it
290	catches and run the mutation check above. Report hollow tests with the
291	assertion quoted, the mode, and a concrete fix.

6	# Writing copy
7	
8	Load `unslop` and `plain-writing` first, then apply these six rules.
9	
10	1. **No eyebrow lines.** Omit the small label or kicker above a heading or
11	   title unless the request asks for one.
12	2. **Question every piece of text.** Name the question it answers and whether
13	   anyone is really asking it. People usually are not. Cut it if not.
14	3. **Keep jargon out of explainers.** One word per idea, defined once. Reuse
15	   that word; do not cycle synonyms.
16	4. **One named audience.** Know who reads it before you write, and write for
17	   that person.
18	5. **No compliance narration.** Do not explain how an action follows a rule
19	   or why it does not break one, unless the reader asked or the action really
20	   sits on the rule's boundary; then state the decision in one clause and stop.
21	   Never explain a distinction the reader set up or plainly knows. After a
22	   correction, report what changed; do not reassure in later messages. The
23	   test: what would the reader misread without this sentence? If nothing, cut
24	   it.
25	6. **Three passes before sending.** Reread the whole draft three times, each
26	   pass with one question: is every claim correct; does every sentence answer
27	   something the reader is asking; is any sentence about the writer rather
28	   than the reader's subject (self-justification, reassurance, credit, effort).
29	   Take the most care with that last kind: it is the easiest to miss in your
30	   own writing. Fix and reread after each pass.

# Unslop

Edit text to remove AI patterns and add human voice.

## Process

1. Scan for the patterns below.
2. Rewrite. Preserve meaning, match intended tone.
3. Add soul (see next section).
4. Self-audit: "What makes this obviously AI generated?" Fix remaining tells.

## Adding soul

Removing patterns is half the job. Sterile, voiceless writing is just as obvious.

- **Have opinions.** React to facts instead of neutrally listing pros and cons.
- **Vary rhythm.** Short sentences. Then longer ones that take their time. Mix it up.
- **Acknowledge complexity.** "Impressive but also kind of unsettling" beats "impressive."
- **Use "I" when it fits.** First person isn't unprofessional.
- **Let some mess in.** Perfect structure looks machine-made.
- **Be specific.** Not "this is concerning" but "there's something unsettling about agents churning away at 3am."

## Patterns to detect and fix

### Content

1. **Puffery.** "pivotal moment", "testament to", "evolving landscape", "setting the stage for", "indelible mark", "deeply rooted". Cut puffery, state what happened.
2. **Name-dropping.** Listing media outlets without context. Pick one, say what was said.
3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.
4. **Promotional language.** "nestled", "vibrant", "breathtaking", "groundbreaking", "renowned", "stunning", "must-visit". Use neutral descriptions.
5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete.
6. **Formulaic challenges.** "Despite challenges... continues to thrive." Replace with specific facts.

### Language

7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Just say "is" or "has".
9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
10. **Unsupported contrasts.** Do not rebut a diagnosis the reader has not made. Remove phrases such as "not X," "rather than X," "as opposed to X," or "this isn't X" unless X was explicitly claimed earlier. Even when a comparison is useful or requested, state the positive evidence and evaluation path instead of negating X. Ask: "Who claimed X?" If the answer is nobody, state the supported fact directly.
11. **Rule of three.** Forcing ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
12. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
13. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.

### Style

13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). Em dashes are an AI tell, and reaching for parentheses instead just trades one tell for another. If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma.
14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example. Not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell.
17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
19. **Curly quotes.** Replace with straight quotes.

### Communication artifacts

20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
21. **Cutoff disclaimers.** "While specific details are limited..." Find sources or remove.
22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.

### Filler

23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". "It is important to note that" gets deleted.
24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may".
25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.

### Jargon

26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate, wedge, vector, locus, vantage, nexus, primitive (as noun), harness (as metaphor), surface (as in "API surface"), bedrock, scaffolding (as metaphor), modality, paradigm, gold-plating, ratchet (as metaphor), evacuate (for moving code), endgame, north star, flywheel. These read as technical but usually have a plainer concrete word. "Substrate" becomes "base". "Wedge in" becomes "add". "Vector" becomes "way" or "method". "Gold-plating" becomes "more than the job needs". "Ratchet" becomes the mechanism's real name or "a limit that only tightens". "Evacuate" becomes "move out". "Endgame" becomes "the last phase". Pick the concrete word.

### Plain speech

27. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the database stays close at hand", "SQL you can read", "types that follow your schema" name a feeling. The fix names the mechanism or a number: "`.toSQL()` returns the exact string sent to the database", "a column rename fails the build". Ask what the sentence tells the reader to do or know, then write that. If you can't restate it as a concrete instruction, fact, or number, cut it. One more check: if the sentence could appear unchanged in another project's docs, it says nothing about this one. Cut it.
28. **Shorten or split dense sentences.** If the reader has to backtrack to parse a sentence, break it in two or drop clauses. One idea per sentence.
29. **Active voice.** Prefer it. Catch "is/are/was/were + past participle" and name the actor: "queries are validated" becomes "the compiler validates queries", "the file is parsed by the loader" becomes "the loader parses the file". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter.
30. **Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb.** "runs quickly" becomes "is fast" or the number. "significantly improves" becomes the measured delta. An adverb propping up a weak verb means the verb is wrong.
31. **Prefer the plain word.** "utilize" becomes "use", "leverage" becomes "use", "facilitate" becomes "help", "numerous" becomes "many", "in the event that" becomes "if". The fancier synonym is rarely clearer.

# Plain writing

Write plain and direct. Apply from the first sentence, to your own replies and
summaries as much as to drafts you're handed.

## Three vices to cut

**1. Deep jargon.** An acronym or insider term used without defining it, or
several undefined terms stacked in one sentence. Define each term in a few plain
words on first use, or don't use it. Covers corporate shorthand, not just
technical terms.
- No: "We'll leverage the Q3 GTM motion to move the needle on NRR."
- Yes: "In the third quarter we'll aim the sales plan at getting current
  customers to spend more."
- Reuse the short form after one definition: "annual recurring revenue (ARR) —
  the subscription income we count on each year" then "ARR."

**2. Throat-clearing.** Preamble and narration about what the text is about to
do. Don't announce structure, editorialize your reasoning, or warm up. Cut "it's
worth being concrete," "before we get into it," "the honest truth is," "this is
the part that matters most."
- No: "Before the details, it's worth stepping back. The honest truth is
  onboarding is broken."
- Yes: "Onboarding is broken: four in ten new users quit before finishing setup."
- Cousin — claiming a virtue instead of showing it: "the honest answer," "to be
  fair," "frankly," "the real question." Delete the label, keep the sentence.

**3. Showing off.** Flourish that sounds clever instead of informing. No
rhetorical triads, aphorisms, italics for drama, cute headings, or punchline
sentences. Cut any sentence doing rhetorical work rather than carrying
information.
- No: "We shipped fast, we shipped hard, and we shipped it *beautiful*."
- Yes: "We shipped the redesign in six weeks."
- Also cut the stacked "not X; Y" antithesis and the punchy fragment for emphasis
  ("Users absorb that as normal. It isn't.").

## Two positive rules

- Plain words, active voice, one idea per sentence in the opening.
- Readable, not dry: lead with a concrete example and keep the prose flowing.

## Mechanics

- Active voice: "The team missed the deadline," not "was missed by the team."
  Passive only when the actor is unknown or irrelevant.
- Present tense for what a thing does: "This setting hides the sidebar."
- Address the reader as "you." "We" only for shared work you're part of.
- Condition before instruction: "If payment fails, retry once."
- One idea per sentence: split on a second "and" or a load-bearing "which."
- Define a term on first use: long form, short form in parentheses, then short
  form.
- Cut reader-blaming softeners: "simply," "just," "easy," "obviously," "of
  course."
- Cut filler openers: "It's worth noting that," "Basically," "At the end of the
  day."
- Sentence case for headings.
- Unambiguous dates: "2026-08-20" or "August 20, 2026," never "08/09."
- Technical writing: code, commands, filenames, and literals in monospace; UI
  names in bold.

## Cutting length

Revision bloats through repetition: a reframing gets patched into every section,
and one claim ends up stated five ways. Reading straight through won't catch it;

import android.content.SharedPreferences
import ly.com.tahaben.notification_filter_domain.schedule.AutomationError
import ly.com.tahaben.notification_filter_domain.schedule.AutomationReceipt

import javax.inject.Inject
import javax.inject.Singleton

/** The last automation outcome, three scalar keys. Unknown stored names read as "no receipt" rather than throwing. */
@Singleton
class SharedPreferencesReceiptStore @Inject constructor(private val preferences: SharedPreferences) : AutomationReceiptStore {
    override fun last(): AutomationReceipt? {
        val at = preferences.getLong(AT, -1L).takeIf { it >= 0 } ?: return null
        val mode = preferences.getString(MODE, null)?.let { name -> ScheduleMode.entries.firstOrNull { it.name == name } }
        val error = preferences.getString(ERROR, null)?.let { name -> AutomationError.entries.firstOrNull { it.name == name } }
        return AutomationReceipt(at, mode, error)
    }

    override fun record(receipt: AutomationReceipt) {
        preferences.edit().putLong(AT, receipt.atEpochMillis).putString(MODE, receipt.mode?.name)
            .putString(ERROR, receipt.error?.name).apply()
    }

    private companion object {
        const val AT = "notification_automation_last_at_v1"
        const val MODE = "notification_automation_last_mode_v1"
        const val ERROR = "notification_automation_last_error_v1"
    }
}

# Settings portability checks

Use this checklist whenever adding settings, changing storage or changing import/export. The prior notification pilot found separate schedule/budget writes and untested Android routing could pass domain tests while phone behavior stayed wrong (`notification-spec-review.md`). Portability adds the same risks across more stores.

- Every user-facing setting has a storage key/type or configuration-table row in the transfer catalog. New settings must register here, or explicitly declare why they are device state rather than configuration.
- SharedPreferences, DataStore and Room configuration participate in the same snapshot. A Settings screen alone does not prove all stores are covered.
- Secret/internal/history keys have positive exclusion fixtures. Automation credentials are regenerated and automation disabled on restore. The old DB-combine flag, live PendingIntents, source event/session keys, onboarding and usage counters are not imported as user intent.
- Unknown legacy keys are reported by name for mapping; their values are not blindly applied. Do not call a partial export complete without reporting unsupported settings.
- Literal legacy data verifies types, exact longs, string sets, app/category/channel keys and schedule/budget values. Malformed schedules raise an error; never replace with a default.
- The production export, rescue conversion and import paths use the tested format and validation. Android runtime wiring gets its own evidence; pure tests do not prove it.
- Import validates the entire document before staging; journal persistence precedes close/restart acknowledgment. Cold-start apply and rollback finish before workers, listener and UI can read stores. Store failures and process interruption preserve recovery.
- History SQL tables and source app files remain untouched. Raw copied DB/WAL data stays only in private temporary storage and is deleted on every exit path.
- Wireless pairing codes, ADB keys and private configuration values never enter logs, crash attachments or repository fixtures. The helper has no public command-execution surface.
- Signing-key-change instructions secure and inspect the backup before removing the old installation. No successful phone recovery claim without an actual source->file->import check.
# Settings recovery feasibility

The owner confirmed the prior installation should be debuggable and wants settings only, excluding notification and usage history. Recovery must read the prior package before any signature-change uninstall. ADB pairing itself does not grant arbitrary app-private-file access: AOSP run-as rejects packages not marked debuggable ([implementation](https://android.googlesource.com/platform/system/core/+/master/run-as/run-as.cpp)). The helper must probe this and report the actual result, not assume success.

The separate rescue app can use Android 11+ same-device wireless pairing, then a raw non-PTY ADB exec stream for run-as reads. Host/port and six-digit pairing code are entered locally in the helper. Pairing and normal connection use different ports; official workstation setup documents the distinction ([Android ADB guide](https://developer.android.com/tools/adb)). No phone recovery or pairing has occurred in this session.

Candidate client: pinned libadb-android 3.1.1, dual Apache-2.0/GPL-3.0-or-later with transitive LGPL notice. Its API supports pair, connect and openStream with arbitrary ADB service destinations ([tagged README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MuntashirAkon/libadb-android/3.1.1/README.md)). Include license notices in rescue. Its SslUtils explicitly prefers the bundled org.conscrypt provider when present ([source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MuntashirAkon/libadb-android/3.1.1/libadb/src/main/java/io/github/muntashirakon/adb/SslUtils.java)); therefore prefer the documented custom Conscrypt dependency rather than device hidden-API exemptions. Same-device pairing remains a device test, not a verified claim.

The upstream pairing implementation opens a Socket and performs blocking TLS/readFully without a socket timeout, and its manager holds a lock while pairing ([pairing source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MuntashirAkon/libadb-android/3.1.1/libadb/src/main/java/io/github/muntashirakon/adb/PairingConnectionCtx.java), [manager source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MuntashirAkon/libadb-android/3.1.1/libadb/src/main/java/io/github/muntashirakon/adb/AbsAdbConnectionManager.java)). Coroutine timeout alone cannot promise to cancel that I/O. Keep rescue jobs bounded with a real cancellation mechanism, e.g. isolate the bridge in a private worker process that can be stopped, or choose a client version providing explicit socket ownership/timeouts. Do not invent a new ADB protocol to solve it. The helper only needs loopback, not arbitrary remote hosts.

Local build constraints: nixed is ARM and currently has about 1.2 GiB available with 3 GiB swap occupied. Its checkout flake and nixpkgs aapt package support Linux x86_64, not Linux ARM. No adb/JDK/Gradle binary is on PATH. sonic SSH timed out. Boat is below the reserve; the prior ten-minute exception is exhausted. Prepare a JVM-only test runner through qex where feasible; Android APK builds still require a viable x86 build route or a fresh bounded owner exception. Never report unrun tests or unpaired recovery as complete.
